title: Surgical treatment of cryptorchidism: current insights and future directions
condition_or_topic: Surgical management of cryptorchidism in children
clinical_background: Cryptorchidism affects approximately 1-5% of full-term boys at birth in Western Countries. Its incidence falls by approximately 50% during the first six months of life as some testes descend spontaneously. Persistent cryptorchidism is associated with impaired fertility and testicular cancer risk, making timely recognition and treatment important. Congenital cryptorchidism warrants early intervention, while retractile testes and acquired cryptorchidism may also affect fertility potential. Surgical decisions depend in part on testicular location and mobility; the best approach to intra-abdominal testes and the role of hormonal therapy remain debated.
objectives: Review surgical treatments for cryptorchidism and their effects on testicular development and function in light of the Nordic consensus statement and current European Association of Urology (EAU) and American Urological Association (AUA) guidelines.
Examine whether recent advances in operative techniques warrant changes to existing protocols.
Describe the operative techniques currently used for intra-abdominal testes.
Assess whether hormonal therapy is an effective adjunct to orchidopexy.
Examine how the EAU, AUA, and Nordic consensus guidelines address these treatment considerations.
study_design: Literature review of surgical treatment for cryptorchidism. PubMed was searched on 9.8.2023, yielding 2933 records; restricting publication dates to 2011 onwards yielded 1165. Titles were screened for relevance, followed by assessment of abstracts. For specific questions, the authors focused on comparative studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses.

population.description: The literature concerned boys with cryptorchidism, including palpable and intra-abdominal undescended testes. The review did not enroll a patient cohort.
inclusion_criteria: Publications from 2011 onwards relevant to surgical treatment of cryptorchidism.
Comparative studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses were prioritized for specific research questions.

interventions: Operative techniques for cryptorchidism, including approaches to intra-abdominal testes.
Hormonal therapy as a possible adjunct to orchidopexy.
interpretation: Early orchidopexy appears to support testicular growth and fertility potential, although later fertility difficulties may still occur. For palpable cryptorchidism, open single-stage orchidopexy is established; a single-incision approach appears promising for lower-positioned testes, but its superiority over two incisions is unresolved. For non-palpable testes, maintaining blood supply is important to limit atrophy. Gubernaculum-sparing second-stage FS orchidopexy and the Shehata technique show promise but require further study. Hormonal treatment remains controversial, and possible benefits must be weighed against adverse effects and delays to surgery.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: The review relates its interpretation of early surgery to the systematic review by Allin et al., which found greater testicular volume and more spermatogonia per tubule after earlier orchidopexy, without a difference in atrophy rates. The systematic reviews summarized in the article generally report favorable outcomes for staged FS procedures, but Tian et al. reported a lower two-stage FS success rate than the other three reviews and a higher overall success rate with the Shehata technique. Findings on gubernaculum preservation are encouraging, although the cited studies do not establish a definitive preferred approach. The review also contrasts guideline advice against routine hormonal treatment with proposals from Hadziselimovic et al. for its use in selected boys at high risk of infertility and azoospermia.
clinical_implications: Congenital, acquired and retractile undescended testes may have implications for fertility potential; even unilateral cryptorchidism may be accompanied by changes in both testes.
Earlier orchidopexy may improve markers of testicular development without eliminating the possibility of later fertility problems.
Testicular position, mobility and vascular supply affect the choice of surgical approach and the feasibility of bringing the testis into the scrotum.
Preservation of blood supply may reduce testicular atrophy. The review associates single-stage laparoscopic orchidopexy that sacrifices the gubernaculum and its vessels with greater atrophy risk.
Hormonal treatment may benefit particular patients, but evidence concerning fertility and cancer outcomes is limited and adverse effects are possible.
practice_implications: Use clinical examination for initial assessment and refer after diagnosis without allowing imaging to delay referral; reserve imaging for selected circumstances in which it could affect surgical planning.
Arrange timely treatment for congenital undescended testes. The guidelines discussed recommend intervention between 6 to 18 months of age.
Use open orchidopexy for palpable testes; a single scrotal incision may be suitable for selected lower-positioned testes, without assuming that it is definitively superior to a two-incision approach.

Base the approach to non-palpable testes and the choice between single-stage and staged surgery on testicular location, mobility, blood supply and surrounding anatomy, in line with the relevant guidelines.

Do not use hormonal therapy routinely as primary treatment for cryptorchidism. Exceptional or selected adjunctive use may be considered, but the review notes that supporting evidence is not yet compelling.

Maintain long-term follow-up to assess fertility outcomes, testicular malignancy risk and psychological effects, and continue to follow existing guidelines while evidence on newer techniques develops.
limitations: Research on gubernaculum-sparing laparoscopic orchidopexy is sparse; the review identified six original studies, of which three were comparative.
Studies of postoperative hormonal therapy have small samples and inconsistent findings, limiting the strength of recommendations.
Evidence does not establish definitive superiority of single-incision over two-incision surgery for palpable testes.
Evidence on the effects of hormonal treatment on infertility or cancer is limited.
open_questions: Whether newer gubernaculum-sparing and traction-based approaches should be incorporated into guidelines remains unsettled.
The optimal role of hormonal therapy, including which patients might benefit as an adjunct to surgery, remains uncertain.
The precise contribution of temperature to impaired spermatogenesis in cryptorchidism remains debated.
future_directions: Conduct further studies to confirm the benefits and limitations of gubernaculum-sparing second-stage FS orchidopexy and the Shehata technique.
Undertake larger trials of postoperative hormonal therapy in selected patient groups to determine whether recommendations can be supported.
Investigate both the potential benefits and the risks of hormonal therapy, including possible infertility and delays to surgery.
Continue long-term evaluation of fertility, testicular malignancy risk and psychological outcomes after treatment.

main_conclusion: The authors regard orchidopexy as the established treatment for cryptorchidism, with operative approach guided by testicular position. Gubernaculum-sparing surgery and the Shehata technique appear promising for challenging non-palpable testes, but stronger evidence is needed before guidelines change; hormonal treatment remains controversial.
narrative_summary: This review examined surgical management of cryptorchidism, including operative timing, palpable and intra-abdominal testes, adjunctive hormonal treatment, and EAU, AUA and Nordic guidance. The authors searched PubMed on 9.8.2023, narrowed the search to publications from 2011 onwards, and assessed relevant comparative studies and reviews. The guidelines discussed recommend intervention between 6 to 18 months of age. Clinical examination is the primary assessment; imaging is reserved for selected situations and should not delay referral. For palpable testes, open orchidopexy is established. A single scrotal incision may suit lower-positioned testes, although its definitive superiority over a two-incision approach has not been established. Intra-abdominal testes may require staged surgery when vessel length limits mobilization. In the cited review by Tian et al., the table reports success rates of 66% for Two-stage FS and 87% for Shehata. Gubernaculum-sparing approaches may help preserve blood supply, but the authors consider the evidence insufficient for their adoption into guidelines. Hormonal therapy is not recommended as primary treatment by the guidelines discussed, although selected adjunctive use remains under investigation. The review reports virilizing effects more frequently with hCG (74%) than with LHRH (5.1%). The authors emphasize timely surgery, adherence to current guidance and long-term follow-up to assess fertility, malignancy risk and psychological impact.

notable_adverse_events: A cited review by Wayne et al. associated two-stage FS, but not one-stage FS, with ileus, hematoma and infection; rates were not provided.
Virilizing effects were reported more frequently with hCG (74%) than with LHRH (5.1%).

The article reports interstitial testicular bleeding and germ cell apoptosis among documented effects of hormone therapy, without assigning these effects to a specific hormone or providing rates. Germ cell apoptosis was associated with reduced testicular volume later in adulthood.

subgroup_analyses: For low palpable cryptorchidism, the cited review by Yu et al. favored single-incision over traditional two-incision orchidopexy. The article notes similar postoperative retraction and atrophy outcomes for the approaches overall and suggests that a single incision may be better suited to lower testes with longer cords; it supplies no comparative rates.

Thorup et al. divided patients with bilateral cryptorchidism into (I) primary testicular failure, (II) transient hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal dysfunction and (III) normal endocrine and histopathologic evaluation. Patients in the transient-dysfunction group might benefit from postoperative hormonal therapy; no effect estimate is given.
The article states that descent following hCG or LHRH treatment is more likely when the testis starts in a more inferior position; it provides no location-specific rates.
The cited review by Gates et al. found similar ascent and atrophy rates for one- and two-stage FS, without supplying subgroup rates.
secondary_results: In Western Countries, cryptorchidism affects approximately 1-5% of full-term boys at birth; its incidence falls by approximately 50% during the first six months of life as testes descend naturally.
A cited histological study found impaired transformation from Ad spermatogonia to Ap spermatogonia in 70% of scrotal testes among patients with unilateral cryptorchidism.
In Dutch schoolboys, the cited prevalence of acquired undescended testis was 1.2% at age 6 years, 2.2% at age 9 years and 1.1% at age of 13 years.
Previously normal testicular positions had been documented in 66% of boys with acquired cryptorchidism in a cited study.
The article cites epididymal and ductus deferens abnormalities in over 50% of patients with cryptorchidism and testisepididymis dissociation in 45-80%.
A cited retrospective cohort by Boehme et al. attributed more than half of orchidopexies performed after the first year of life to acquired undescended testis.
Hack et al. postulated that acquired cryptorchidism occurs three times more frequently than primary cryptorchidism.
A cited German retrospective study of over 3500 patients reported that 42% of orchidopexies during 2003-2012 were performed at ages 4 to 17 years; the acquired-disease proportion was unclear.
The article reports documented success rates between 80-86% for staged FS in its introductory discussion.
The cited review by Gates et al. included 260 articles and associated surgery before one year of age with better testicular growth and potential fertility than later surgery.

The article states that the G/T ratio is better preserved after early orchidopexy. It also describes an association between serum inhibin-B and G/T and reports that low serum inhibin-B in boys with bilateral cryptorchidism can predict a compromised G/T, without numerical estimates.

The article reports that, in all studies, the single-stage laparoscopic approach sacrificing the gubernaculum and its associated vessels was associated with a greater risk of testicular atrophy, without providing a pooled effect estimate.

document_sections.content: Cryptorchidism has an incidence of 1-5% and may affect later fertility and health. This review examines surgical approaches and their effects on testicular development and function alongside the Nordic consensus statement and European Association of Urology (EAU) and American Urological Association (AUA) guidelines. Congenital and acquired cryptorchidism present different surgical challenges and fertility implications. Congenital disease warrants early treatment, while retractile testes and acquired disease also merit consideration because of possible fertility risks. Testicular position and age support a practical classification of undescended testes. Clinical examination permits early diagnosis; imaging is appropriate only in selected circumstances. Guidelines recommend orchidopexy at 6-12 months of age for congenital cryptorchidism, and increasing evidence supports early surgery for testicular health and fertility potential. Surgical choices include open and laparoscopic approaches, selected largely according to testicular position and accessibility; limited mobility may require sequential operations. Hormonal therapy has a secondary role and may be considered selectively as an adjunct, but its benefits and limitations require further study. Long-term follow-up is important for assessing fertility, testicular malignancy risk and psychological effects.

document_sections.heading: 1 Introduction
document_sections.content: Cryptorchidism affects approximately 1-5% of full-term boys at birth in Western Countries and means that one or both testes have not reached the scrotum. Its incidence falls by approximately 50% during the first six months through spontaneous descent; persistent cases require clinical intervention. Untreated cryptorchidism increases the risks of impaired fertility and testicular cancer. Early treatment can substantially reduce, and potentially eliminate, those risks. Although the scrotum's cooler environment is thought necessary for spermatogenesis, the precise contribution of temperature remains disputed. Stem-cell niches require tightly controlled conditions for cell propagation and differentiation. Despite uncertainty about the biological mechanisms, orchidopexy remains the principal intervention. After orchidopexy, the germ cells per tubular cross-section ration (G/T) can indicate fertility potential: a lower ratio signals greater infertility risk, including in unilateral disease. Sertoli cells produce Inhibin-B, an indicator of seminiferous-tubule function; serum levels correlate with prepubertal Sertoli-cell counts and strongly with G/T. Recent research suggests that low serum inhibin-B reliably predicts impaired G/T in bilateral cryptorchidism. Histology indicates that unilateral disease can affect both testes: 70% of scrotal testes in patients with unilateral cryptorchidism showed impaired transformation of Ad spermatogonia into Ap spermatogonia. Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism can cause cryptorchidism but is relatively uncommon compared with cryptorchidism overall. Gonadotropins vary substantially during minipuberty, making precise age-matched measurements important; available studies suggest hypergonadotropism rather than hypogonadotropism. Current guidelines therefore reserve gonadotropin/Gonadotropin hormone releasing hormone (GNRH) treatment mainly for clinical hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, not routine cryptorchidism treatment. Congenital disease raises infertility risk and calls for early intervention. Retractile testes and acquired cryptorchidism may also affect fertility, to differing degrees. Mobility informs treatment decisions, while emerging evidence suggests that acquired disease may have greater fertility implications than previously thought; reported histological changes resemble those in congenital disease. Careful management of all forms is consequently relevant to reducing fertility risk. Among Dutch schoolboys, acquired undescended testis prevalence was 1.2% at age 6 years, 2.2% at age 9 years and 1.1% at age of 13 years. In 66% of boys with acquired cryptorchidism, earlier records placed the testes normally, supporting continued examination throughout childhood. Fetal testicular descent is biphasic and involves complex physiological changes. The gubernaculum is important in both phases but can occasionally elongate the epididymis. Over 50% of patients with cryptorchidism have epididymal or ductus deferens abnormalities; testisepididymis dissociation, reported in 45-80%, is thought to reflect a persistently abnormal genital mesentery. Surgeons need to recognize these anatomical variations. Early detection and repair before 1 year of age remain the most important measures for limiting harm in unilateral and bilateral disease. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, Allin et al. found no difference in atrophy between orchidopexy before and after one year, but earlier surgery was associated with greater testicular volume and more spermatogonia per tubule across fifteen eligible studies, suggesting better fertility potential. A retrospective cohort study by Boehme et al. attributed more than half of orchidopexies after the first year to acquired undescended testes. Hack et al. proposed in a Netherlands study from 2003 that acquired cryptorchidism occurs three times as often as primary disease. A German retrospective study of over 3500 patients found that 42% of orchidopexies during 2003-2012 involved patients aged 4 to 17 years; the acquired proportion was unclear. One-stage orchidopexy preserving spermatic vessels is standard for palpable inguinal testes. Short spermatic vessels often restrict mobilization of intra-abdominal testes, leaving the optimal one-stage or two-stage strategy debated. In one-stage surgery, the testis is moved directly into the scrotum during one operation, with possible spermatic-vessel division. In two-stage surgery, vessels are divided first and scrotal placement follows at a second operation. The staged Fowler and Stephens (FS) approach, introduced in 1959, is commonly used for high intra-abdominal testes when vessel tension prevents mobilization. Vessel ligation may, however, cause atrophy; reported success is between 80-86%. The Shehata technique uses traction-induced elongation to improve mobilization while preserving vascular supply. Ellis et al. reported that the gubernaculum contributes to blood supply alongside the spermatic vessels and vas deferens. Gubernaculum-sparing FS orchidopexy consequently aims to support testicular survival while preserving cremasteric collateral vessels. The review evaluates surgical methods in relation to the Nordic consensus statement and current EAU and AUA guidelines.

document_sections.heading: 2 Methodology
document_sections.content: The authors searched PubMed on 9.8.2023 for surgical treatment of cryptorchidism, using combinations of operative or surgical-treatment terms and cryptorchidism-related terms. The general search yielded 2933 results. Restricting publication dates to 2011 onwards reduced the results to 1165. Titles were screened for relevance, followed by abstract assessment; for specific questions, attention focused on comparative studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses. The review asked whether newer operative methods warrant changes to existing protocols, which techniques are used for intraabdominal testes, whether hormonal therapy is an effective adjunct to orchidopexy, and how the EAU, AUA and Nordic consensus guidelines address these issues.

document_sections.heading: 3 Guideline policies for orchidopexy
document_sections.content: Physical examination is the primary means of assessment. For a non-palpable testis, ultrasound can help when its findings would determine the operative approach or whether diagnostic laparoscopy is needed. Imaging should otherwise be selective and must not postpone referral after diagnosis. EAU, AUA and Nordic Consensus guidelines all recommend intervention between 6 to 18 months of age. For palpable undescended testes, the AUA favors a standard inguinal approach; EAU and Nordic Consensus guidance also accepts a scrotal approach in selected cases. For nonpalpable testes, EAU and Nordic guidance favors laparoscopy, whereas the AUA accepts open or laparoscopic surgery. The AUA leaves the one-stage versus twostage decision to the surgeon, informed by testicular position, vascular supply and adjacent anatomy. The EAU suggests a two-stage approach might reduce atrophy and improve mobility. EAU and AUA guidance does not recommend hormonal therapy as primary treatment. Nordic guidance likewise notes limited effectiveness and possible adverse effects in childhood, although it allows consideration in exceptional cases; convincing evidence for benefit before or after surgery remains lacking. All three sets of guidance stress long-term follow-up.

document_sections.heading: 4 Impact of orchidopexy timing on testicular characteristics
document_sections.content: Cryptorchid testes often have lower volume and morphological abnormalities, including diffuse hypoechogenicity, microlithiasis and an irregular surface. Testicular position may influence atrophy more than age at surgery. Younger patients had fewer morphological abnormalities (25.0% vs 83.3%, p=0.05), although mean testicular volume ratio did not differ significantly between surgery before and after two years of age. Earlier orchidopexy better preserves G/T. Allin et al.'s systematic review likewise associated earlier surgery with larger testes and more spermatogonia per tubule, suggesting better fertility potential, but subsequent fertility difficulties can still occur.

document_sections.heading: 5 Palpable testes
document_sections.content: Primary open orchidopexy for palpable testes has high success rates and represents the current consensus approach. Two-incision inguinal and single scrotal incision procedures have similar postoperative retraction and atrophy outcomes; the single-incision approach appears better suited to lower testes with longer cords. Technique selection rests with the surgeon. Studies from Canada and Saudi Arabia reported that pediatric urologists tend to prefer a single incision when appropriate. In a systematic review and meta-analysis, Yu et al. found advantages for single-incision over traditional two-incision orchidopexy and proposed it as the first choice for low palpable cryptorchidism.

document_sections.heading: 6 Intra-abdominal testes
document_sections.content: The review identified four systematic reviews concerning two-stage procedures for intra-abdominal testes (IAT). TABLE 1 presents success rates for direct and staged FowlerStephens orchidopexies and the Shehata technique across the cited reviews. Penson et al. reviewed studies from 1980-2012 to assess hormonal and surgical treatment. They found fourteen hormonal-therapy studies and 26 surgical-outcome studies, with 695 participants undergoing primary orchidopexy, 644 undergoing 1-stage FS and 784 undergoing 2-stage FS orchidopexy. They judged hormonal therapy alone only marginally effective relative to placebo, though potentially useful for some patients. Their reported surgical success rates were 96.4% for primary orchidopexy, 78.7% for 1stage Fowler-Stephens and 86% for 2-stage FS orchidopexy. Descent and outcome rates were comparable for primary and laparoscopic interventions. Wayne et al. reviewed intra-abdominal testis management and fertility preservation during 2008-2014, identifying two systematic reviews and 29 nonrandomized studies. They reported 85-100% success for primary orchidopexy in low IAT, compared with 8085% for FS orchidopexy. Two stage FS was associated with ileus, hematoma and infection, unlike one-stage FS in their review. At 10-17 years after two-stage FS, 83% of testes were scrotal. Gates et al. reviewed evidence from 2005-2020 on imaging, medical care, operative techniques, timing and outcomes, including 260 articles. They reserved preoperative imaging and hormonal therapy for special circumstances and suggested surgery before one year of age because it improves testicular growth and potential fertility compared with later surgery. They reported similar ascent and atrophy rates for one-stage and two-stage FS. Tian et al. compared FS with Shehata in a systematic review and meta-analysis of four studies published during 2021-2022, with 77 and 69 participants in the respective groups. They found higher overall success with Shehata than staged FS, but similar operative times and retraction rates. The two-stage FS success rate in their analysis was 66%, lower than in the other three systematic reviews.

document_sections.heading: 7 Gubernaculum sparing laparoscopic orchidopexy
document_sections.content: Evidence on gubernaculum-sparing laparoscopic orchidopexy is limited: the authors identified six original studies, three comparative. TABLE 2 shows absence-of-atrophy and absence-of-ascent outcomes for staged procedures involving gubernaculum preservation and comparator operations. In a prospective comparison with treatment determined by surgeon preference, Braga et al. assessed gubernaculum-sparing orchidopexy against conventional laparoscopic FS to improve perfusion and reduce atrophy. Among 212 intraabdominal testes, 46 underwent conventional FS and 166 underwent gubernaculum sparing laparoscopic orchidopexy. Atrophy occurred in 28.3% after conventional FS versus 0.6% after the gubernaculum-sparing procedure, p<0.01. Distance from the internal inguinal ring did not predict atrophy; the investigators concluded that preserving cremasteric vessels may improve outcomes. Roy et al. retrospectively evaluated two-stage FS in 128 intra-abdominal testes, with 96 available for follow-up. Successful outcomes occurred in 85%. They identified no clear predictors of success or intraoperative or operative risk factors for outcome, but hypothesized that gubernaculum preservation might lower atrophy risk (p=0.06; OR 3; 95% CI 0.97-9.3). Zhou et al. retrospectively compared open and laparoscopic gubernaculum-sparing second-stage FS in 205 patients, of whom 96 underwent the gubernaculum-sparing procedure. Overall atrophy was 1.5%; postoperative ascent occurred in 2.8% and 3.1% in the respective groups. They detected no significant between-group difference and considered gubernaculum-sparing FS survival and outcomes comparable with more invasive open surgery.

document_sections.heading: 8 Hormonal therapy in conjunction with surgical intervention
document_sections.content: Hormonal therapy remains disputed. The Nordic Consensus, EAU and AUA advise against hormone therapy for cryptorchidism. Descent after human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG) or luteinizing hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) depends strongly on initial testicular position: a lower starting position increases the chance of descent. Evidence concerning cancer and infertility outcomes is limited. In contrast, Hadziselimovic et al. advocate hormonal therapy as primary treatment, arguing that it can avoid surgery and, in nonresponders, facilitate testicular fixation and markedly reduce postoperative atrophy. They recommend it for boys at high risk of infertility and azoospermia after early orchidopexy. Thorup et al. classified bilateral cryptorchidism using testicular mass, germ-cell number, maturation to Ad Spermatogonia and hormone levels. Their groups were (I) primary testicular failure, (II) transient hypothalamus-pituitary-gonadal dysfunction and (III) normal endocrine and histopathologic evaluation. They suggested that patients with temporary hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal dysfunction might benefit from postoperative hormonal treatment. Current studies suggest possible benefit in selected groups, but small samples and inconsistent results preclude compelling recommendations without larger trials. Hildorf et al. found serum inhibin-B below the 2.5 percentile in 11% of boys with unilateral cryptorchidism, consistent with infertility risk anticipated from long-term follow-up. Among these patients, 90% showed transient hypogonadotropic hypogonadism, which might affect both testes even when one descends spontaneously and the other is surgically positioned. Adjuvant gonadotropin-releasing hormone may be considered for such patients. Hormonal treatment can cause adverse effects: virilizing effects were reported more often with hCG (74%) than with LHRH (5.1%). Many systemic effects are transient and resolve within six months, but reported testicular effects include interstitial bleeding and germ-cell apoptosis, associated with lower testicular volume in adulthood.

document_sections.heading: 9 Conclusion
document_sections.content: Orchidopexy remains central to pediatric urologic surgery while techniques continue to develop. For palpable cryptorchidism, open single-stage surgery is established and safe. Available evidence cautiously favors a single incision for lower testes, but superiority over two incisions is not definitive. Non-palpable disease remains difficult to treat, and maintaining perfusion is important for preventing atrophy. Gubernaculum-sparing secondstage FS and the Shehata variant appear promising but require further research. Across the studies discussed, single-stage laparoscopic orchidopexy that sacrifices the gubernaculum and its associated vessels was linked to greater atrophy risk. Hormonal treatment remains controversial: it may have therapeutic value, but possible infertility and delays to surgery require further investigation. Hormonal assessment may eventually complement orchidopexy and support more individualized treatment. Emerging laparoscopic methods need stronger evidence before guideline inclusion. Existing guideline-aligned care continues to produce excellent outcomes, making adherence to current guidance important.
